questions.question_text: Which property is enough to identify a solid as a prism?

options.text: It has the same cross-section parallel to its base throughout.
It has at least one triangular face.
options.why: Treats any triangular face as proof of a pyramid or prism.

options.text: It has exactly one base.
options.why: Uses the defining base count of a pyramid instead of a prism.

options.text: Its faces meet at one apex.
options.why: Uses the defining apex property of a pyramid.

questions.solution_text: A prism has a uniform cross-section parallel to its base.

options.text: It is a pyramid because its side faces meet at one apex.
It is a prism because it has flat faces.
options.why: Treats having flat faces as sufficient, although both families have flat faces.

options.text: It is a prism because its base is a pentagon.
options.why: Uses the base shape but ignores that there is only one base and an apex.

options.text: It is a pyramid because it has two matching bases.
options.why: Attributes the prism base property to a pyramid.

questions.solution_text: The side faces meet at a single apex, so the solid is a pyramid.

questions.question_text:
A solid has two identical parallel hexagonal ends.
What must be true?

options.text: It is a hexagonal prism.
It is a hexagonal pyramid.
options.why: Uses pyramid even though a pyramid has only one base.

options.text: It is a triangular prism.
options.why: Counts the joining faces instead of naming the base shape.

options.text: It cannot be classified.
options.why: Ignores that two matching parallel bases determine a prism.

questions.solution_text: Two identical parallel hexagonal bases identify a hexagonal prism.

questions.question_text: What happens to cross-sections parallel to the base of a pyramid as they approach the apex?

options.text: They keep the same shape but become smaller.
They stay the same shape and size.
options.why: Uses the uniform-cross-section property of a prism.

options.text: They become larger than the base.
options.why: Reverses the taper towards the apex.

options.text: They change into rectangles.
options.why: Assumes the side-face shape becomes the cross-section.

questions.solution_text: Parallel slices shrink towards the apex while keeping the base shape.

options.text: A prism has two matching bases; a pyramid has one base and an apex.
A prism has one base; a pyramid has two matching bases.
options.why: Reverses the base counts of the two solid families.

options.text: Both solids always have two matching bases.
options.why: Transfers the prism property to pyramids.

options.text: Both solids always have one base and an apex.
options.why: Transfers the pyramid property to prisms.

questions.solution_text: The base count and presence of an apex distinguish the two families.

questions.question_text:
A solid has rectangular side faces and two matching triangular ends.
Which feature rules out a pyramid?

options.text: The two matching ends
The triangular ends
options.why: Assumes any triangular face rules out a pyramid, though pyramid side faces are triangular.

options.text: The flat faces
options.why: Uses a property shared by both prisms and pyramids.

options.text: The number of vertices
options.why: Chooses a count that is not supplied in the stem.

questions.solution_text: A pyramid has one base; two matching ends identify a prism.
